title: SAGE: Steerable Adversarial Scenario Generation
one_liner: Train two opposing expert policies and mix their weights at test time to steer between adversarial and realistic driving scenarios without retraining.
lead: Autonomous driving systems need to be tested against dangerous scenarios. Existing methods force you to choose: train for dangerous but unrealistic scenarios, or realistic but safe ones. This paper teaches a model two opposing strategies (push for danger, stay realistic) and lets you dial between them instantly at test time by blending their learned weights, like mixing two paint colors.

problem.h2: Testing autonomous cars with fixed trade-offs
paras: Autonomous cars need to be tested against bad scenarios that might cause crashes. But there are two competing goals: make scenarios dangerous enough to find real problems, and keep them realistic enough that the car's new behaviors actually transfer to real roads. Existing methods train a single model that commits to one fixed balance between these two goals.

A naive approach: train one model to maximize danger (make adversarial scenarios). It works for finding problems, but the scenarios become physically impossible — cars driving through walls, instant 90-degree turns. The trained driving policy learns to handle these fake tricks and fails on real roads. Or train for realism only. Then you get dull scenarios that never stress the system, so the car never learns to handle unexpected edge cases.

callout.html: You want to choose at test time whether a scenario should be more dangerous or more realistic, but retraining the generator for each choice is too slow.

panels.title: 1. The old way: pick one mix
panels.caption: Old method locks in one balance between danger and realism. No choice at test time.

panels.title: 2. Problem: conflicting demands
panels.viz_args: Danger goal vs Realism goal pull opposite ways
panels.caption: Maximizing danger breaks physics. Maximizing realism misses edge cases.

panels.title: 3. SAGE trains two experts
panels.caption: Expert 1: learned to push adversarial scenarios. Expert 2: learned realistic paths.

panels.title: 4. Mix the weights at test time
panels.viz_args: Slide from Expert 1 to Expert 2. No retraining needed.
panels.caption: Blend expert weights. 30 percent danger, 70 percent realism. Done instantly.

panels.title: 5. One model, infinite trade-offs
panels.caption: Dial the mix: dangerous-only, balanced, safe. Each choice costs nothing.

steps.b: Decouple hard rules from soft goals.
steps.text: Separate physical constraints (map boundaries, max acceleration) from competing objectives (danger versus realism).
Teach one policy to favor adversarial scenarios, weighted heavily toward the danger goal.
Teach another policy the opposite preference: favor realistic, feasible scenarios.
Given a user preference dial from pure realism to pure danger, blend the two experts' learned weights in between.
Run the mixed-weight model to produce a scenario with the desired balance, no retraining.

paras: The paper moves the learned weights (the numbers that define what the model does) rather than training a new model. Instead of retraining when you want a different balance, it linearly blends the weight values from the adversary expert and the realist expert.

hidden.name: position on the Pareto front
paras: The hidden quantity is how far along the optimal trade-off curve you are. The Pareto front is the set of all possible balanced scenarios: moving more toward danger means losing realism, moving toward realism means losing danger. No single point dominates all others. This paper measures your position on that curve numerically by the interpolation weight.

The paper estimates this quantity implicitly through the test-time dial. When the user sets the preference weight to 0.3, the model interpolates: 0.3 times Expert Adversary's weights plus 0.7 times Expert Realist's weights. This positions you 30 percent along the spectrum from realism to danger.

heat.caption: Darker: more toward danger. Highlight: key points where trade-off is explicit.

reads.html: The model learned two opposite strategies. At test time, dial a number between 0 and 1. The model blends: a bit of Adversary, a lot of Realist, or anywhere in between.

The paper trains Expert Adversary and Expert Realist on opposing preference objectives, then at test time blends their learned weights using a linear interpolation controlled by the user's preference dial.

mechanism.h2: Why weight interpolation works across the trade-off space
paras: When two expert models are trained from the same starting point on related tasks (both generating driving scenarios, just with different goal weights), their learned weights live in a connected space. Moving in a straight line through weight space from one expert to the other does not hit broken or nonsensical models; instead, it traces a smooth path that represents the full spectrum of trade-offs.

Here is why this works mechanically. During training, Expert Adversary learns which scenario changes and trajectory tweaks lead to crashes, while Expert Realist learns which changes keep things realistic. Both experts learn from the same data, with the same basic model structure. When you linearly interpolate their weights, you are literally mixing their learned intuitions. A weight that both experts set high means both care about that feature — it stays high. A weight where they disagree gets a compromise value. The result is a model that balances the two goals smoothly, without ever retraining. The paper proves this works by showing that when fine-tuned models start from the same initialization on related tasks, there is a smooth, well-behaved path in weight space connecting them — no dead zones where the mixed model breaks.

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Say Expert Adversary learned weight w1 = 0.8 (leans heavily toward danger).
Expert Realist learned w1 = 0.2 (leans toward realism).
User sets mu = 0.4 (wants 40 percent danger, 60 percent realism).
The mixed model uses w1 = 0.44, a middle ground between the two experts.

math.note: The formula simply blends the two trained expert models; no new training happens when the user changes the dial.

charts.title: Old fixed-trade-off method
charts.note: Locked into one balance. If user wants more realism, must retrain from scratch (100% extra time).

charts.title: SAGE with weight interpolation
charts.note: User can dial any mix instantly. Scenarios stay realistic at all points on the curve.

items.html: If the two experts learned extremely different strategies, a straight line between their weights might pass through regions where the mixed model is broken or incoherent. Linear mode connectivity assumes the models were trained on related tasks from the same start, so this is rare, but it can happen if the experts diverge too much.

items.b: Constraints get violated at intermediate mixes.
items.html: Hard rules like map boundaries and maximum acceleration are enforced during training. But if the experts learned to bend the rules in different ways, mixing their weights might produce scenarios that violate physical constraints. This is why the paper separates hard constraints from soft preferences during training.

The interpolation weight is not a direct measure of danger or realism; it is a position in learned weight space. Small dial changes can have large effects if the experts learned different importance for certain details in the scenario.

items.b: Done right: separate constraints and preferences.
items.html: The paper enforces hard rules as data filters during training (only use valid scenarios), then trains experts on soft preferences (the weighted trade-off between danger and realism). This ensures interpolation never breaks physics, only the balance between competing goals.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple scenario generator on a tiny driving domain (e.g., a two-lane road with one other car). Train Expert Adversary to maximize collision likelihood while keeping scenarios valid. Train Expert Realist to minimize speed and acceleration changes. Then, at test time, vary the interpolation weight mu from 0 to 1 (pure realism to pure danger) and collect generated scenarios. Measure danger as probability of collision, and realism as how closely the scenario matches natural driving patterns from a logged dataset.
demo.metric_eq: frontier_quality = (adversarial_scenarios_at_mu * realism_score_at_mu) averaged across all mu in [0, 1]
demo.closing: The demo makes impossible to miss: as you dial the preference slider, scenarios smoothly shift from mundane to perilous, all without retraining the model.
